recipe.history:
The portobello mushroom is not an ancient species but rather a marketing triumph built on top of a genuinely magnificent ingredient. Agaricus bisporus — the common cultivated mushroom — has been grown intentionally since seventeenth-century France, where mushroom farmers near Paris discovered they could cultivate it on beds of composted horse manure in the cool dark tunnels and quarries beneath the city. The small white button mushroom and the cremini are simply younger, less mature versions of the same fungus; a portobello is what happens when Agaricus bisporus is allowed to fully open its cap and develop its gills, concentrating its earthy, savory, umami-rich flavor over additional days of growth. Italy has long embraced the mature version, grilling large caps with olive oil and garlic as a standalone dish, and the name "portobello" is widely believed to have been coined in the 1980s by American marketers looking to rebrand the overgrown brown mushroom that supermarkets couldn't move. Whatever its naming history, the portobello's meaty texture and deep umami profile have made it one of the most respected vegetables in professional kitchens worldwide.

The portobello's journey onto the American burger is a story of the 1990s culinary shift toward vegetarian and flexitarian eating. As health-conscious diners began questioning the daily beef patty, restaurant kitchens started experimenting with mushroom caps as a direct patty substitute — grilled whole, they have a satisfying chew, absorb marinades beautifully, and produce a savory, steamy interior that mimics the experience of biting into a burger. But smart cooks quickly realized the portobello was even better alongside beef than in place of it, layering its earthy depth under and over a proper patty to amplify the burger's savory register. By the early 2000s, the portobello burger topping had become a fixture of gastropub menus and upscale diner specials, a marker of seriousness about ingredients. Sliced and sautéed or grilled in strips — like a belt across the burger — it adds moisture, texture contrast, and an almost meaty second layer to every bite.

I grew up thinking mushrooms were the rubbery grey things that came out of a can and landed on pizza whether you wanted them or not. My genuine appreciation for them started at a farmers market on a rainy Saturday when a vendor handed me a grilled portobello cap on a piece of crusty bread, drizzled with nothing but good olive oil and a pinch of coarse salt. I stood there in the rain eating it and feeling embarrassed that I had spent so many years dismissing this ingredient. The texture was silky and firm at the same time, the flavor was deep and almost smoky from the char, and I kept thinking: this tastes like something that took a long time to get good. I went home and put portobellos on everything for the next month, and eventually they landed on a burger, laid across the patty like a belt, and that was the end of the question.

There is a reason every serious burger cook pulls their patty at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 degrees Celsius, and refuses to go further. At medium rare the beef is still a living, juicy thing — the fat has rendered into the meat, the center glows pink and warm, and every bite releases a cascade of savory liquid that carries the flavors of everything else on the burger. The portobello sautéed alongside it, laid across the top like a savory belt, needs that juicy foundation to make sense; on an overcooked, dry patty it would just be a wet thing on a dry thing. Medium rare is the condition under which all the ingredients on a great burger achieve harmony. To cook beyond it is to choose a lesser meal when a magnificent one was entirely within reach.
ingredients: 1 egg + 1 tbsp water for egg wash
680g ground beef (80/20 chuck blend), freshly ground
2 large portobello mushroom caps, cleaned and sliced into 1/2-inch strips
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine warm milk, sugar, and yeast in the bowl of a stand mixer. Let sit 5 minutes until foamy.
2. Add egg and softened butter. Mix briefly. Add bread flour and salt. Knead with dough hook on medium speed for 8 minutes until smooth and tacky.
3. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and let rise 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled.
4. Divide into 4 portions (~150g each), shape into rounds, place on a parchment-lined sheet, cover, and proof 45 minutes.
5. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash, sprinkle sesame seeds. Bake 16 to 18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on a rack.

6. Make the garlic aioli: Mince garlic finely and then crush to a paste with the flat of a knife and a pinch of salt. Whisk together garlic paste, mayonnaise, lemon juice, and Dijon mustard. Season to taste. Refrigerate until needed.
7. Marinate portobello strips: Toss mushroom strips with olive oil, minced garlic, thyme, balsamic vinegar, salt, and pepper. Let sit at least 15 minutes.

8. Cook the portobello belt: Heat a skillet or grill pan over medium-high heat. Add marinated mushroom strips and cook, turning occasionally, for 6 to 8 minutes until golden, tender, and slightly caramelized. Set aside and keep warm.

9. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (170g each). Form into 3/4-inch thick patties with a dimple pressed in the center. Season on both sides with salt, pepper, and onion powder just before cooking.
10. Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil.
11. Place patties in the pan. Cook 2 minutes undisturbed. Flip once. Immediately top each patty with a slice of provolone.
12. Continue cooking 1.5 to 2 minutes more, tenting with foil to melt cheese, until an instant-read thermometer reads 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Rest on a wire rack 3 minutes.
13. Toast the buns: Butter cut sides and toast face-down in a skillet over medium heat until golden, about 1 minute.
14. Assemble: Spread garlic aioli generously on both cut faces of each bun. Place arugula on the bottom bun, then tomato slices and red onion.
15. Set the medium-rare provolone-topped patty on the vegetables. Drape 3 to 4 strips of sautéed portobello across the top of the patty like a belt.
16. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately.
